proof.criterion: Review round three, blocking: a publish whose context has already ended must put nothing on the wire, on both transports.
proof.surface: A real nats-server with a subscriber on the subject, through bus.Client.PublishWithin: a role lane and an ad-hoc topic (core transport) and an agent subject (JetStream), with the stream read back for the last message on the captured topic.
proof.observed: All four PASS (3.48s and 0.01s): under a deadline already past and under a cancelled context the publish is refused, the subscriber receives nothing and the stream holds nothing, while the control under a live context publishes and is received. The JetStream case is not an abstract assertion about the dependency: usesCoreTransport is asserted false for that topic first, so the case exercises publishJetStream, and the mutation below shows it bites there.
proof.negativeControl: Three mutations, each isolating one check. (1) Dropping nats.Context(ctx) from publishJetStream's options - the upgrade risk the comment names - makes the JetStream case fail with 'publish under a deadline already past succeeded, want it refused', so that half exercises the path rather than the dependency's reputation. (2) Removing publishConfirmed's spent-deadline check fails TestAPublishConfirmedWithASpentDeadlinePublishesNothing with 'publishConfirmed called publish 1 times with its deadline already spent, want none'. (3) Removing publishCoreTo's ctx.Err() check: I drove the two halves directly with a probe, since the end-to-end test stops at its first failing assertion. Under that mutation a deadline already past is still refused by publishConfirmed and the subscriber receives nothing, but a cancelled context whose deadline is still ahead answered nil and THE MESSAGE REACHED THE SUBSCRIBER. So the two checks hold different halves and neither covers for the other: publishConfirmed is given a deadline and cannot see a cancel, and publishCoreTo's own check is what catches it. The implementer's deviation from the architect's one-check ruling is upheld by that measurement. All three reverted.

proof.criterion: The documentation's new claim - 'pushed at most twice' - is what the code does rather than a guarantee it does not hold.
proof.surface: The three places that carry it, read against the code and against the loop driven above.
proof.command: grep -n 'at most twice' docs/architecture.md AGENTS.md CHANGELOG.md cmd/listener/delivery.go; and the loop probe's push count across twelve real deliveries
proof.observed: docs/architecture.md:182, CHANGELOG.md:622 and delivery.go:596 all now say a push that failed is deferred once and the give-up after it is terminal whether or not its notice can be published, so it is pushed at most twice. Driven: twelve real deliveries, two pushes. The bound does not rest on process memory alone, which is what makes the claim safe to state: metadata.NumDelivered is the stream's, so a listener that restarts mid-flight still gives the message up on the delivery after its one deferral (delivery.go:838-841), and the attempt-cache entry the give-up keeps turns away the redelivery a lost ACK brings inside attemptCacheTTL. The one path I can construct past two is a lost ACK and a process restart together - the redelivery would reach a listener with no attempt entry - which is two simultaneous faults, which no claim here covers and which the code comment at the give-up already scopes by naming attemptCacheTTL. Checked, and recorded as a boundary rather than raised as a finding.
proof.negativeControl: The claim was read against the code, not against the old wording: the push bound is pushFailedDeferrals applied at delivery.go:838-841 and the terminal give-up at :894-901, and the removal of either is caught by the mutations recorded above.
